newsitem.title: BELARUS: Ford using air cargo to launch Belarus plant.
newsitem.headline: Ford using air cargo to launch Belarus plant.

text.p: Ford Motor Co, the world's second-largest automaker, has been using air cargo over surface transport for emergency parts shipments from Germany to support the start-up of its vehicle assembly plant in Belarus.

"Air freight is 25 to 50 percent cheaper than ground expeditors," said Douglas Young, materials planning and logistics manager for the plant in Obchuck, six kilometers northeast of the Belarus capital Minsk.

"It is extremely expensive to rush deliveries by road because the trucking companies know that they will sit at the border of Poland and Belarus for two days, and they build that into the price," Young said, speaking to journalists visiting the plant, which is named Ford Union (FU).
"Belarus is one of the few places I know where air freight is cheaper than surface transport," Young said.
FU pays roughly 3,500 marks ($1,910) for a van with a payload of four-to-five tonnes to deliver parts from Cologne, Germany, which is Ford's consolidation centre for shipments to eastern Europe.

The plant, which builds Escort cars and Transit commercial vehicles from imported kits of bodies and parts, is a smaller version of a $50 million plant in Plonsk, Poland, which uses no air cargo, Young said.

Moreover, the Polish plant, pays only 2,000 marks for emergency road shipments from Cologne, he added. That means the per-kilometer payment for ground expeditors from Cologne is roughly 2.0 marks to Plonsk and nearly 2.5 marks to Minsk.
Shippers often use air cargo over sea and surface transport out of necessity. But, ironically, FU must often opt for a road service over an airline, Young said.

"Sometimes parts like bumpers are too big to fit into airplanes flying into Minsk, and sometimes no scheduled flights are available to carry the parts," he said. "Lufthansa flies only once a day, and Austrian Airlines flies only three times a week -- that's really it."
Belarus national carrier Belavia is supposed to fly three times a week to Germany but sometimes goes only once, he added.
FU only uses air cargo for irregular "panic shipments", Young said, adding he hopes to reduce their frequency not long after the plant holds its opening ceremony on July 30.
Ford also expects ground expeditors to become more attractive once the Belarus government opens an alternative road crossing at the Polish border, Young said.

Air cargo services also are improving, as FU has started working with a Belarus freight forwarder that has the right to carry shipments from the airport without any customs clearance until the goods arrive at the factory, he said.
